diagram_classification: theological (Trinitarian diagram combined with a Crucifixion image)
interpretation: The diagram is a Trinitarian figure in the form of an inverted triangle with a circle at each of its three corners. A fourth circle sits at the centre and is joined to the three corner circles by spokes, as in a Y-shaped or tripartite scheme. This arrangement is typical of the 'scutum fidei' (shield of the Trinity) tradition, in which the three outer nodes stand for Father, Son and Holy Spirit and the central node for the shared divine essence or unity (Deus). The circles are empty in the image and any inscriptions are not legible, so the identification of each node as a person of the Trinity is inferred from the form. A crucified Christ hangs from the central circle and extends down toward the bottom circle. This links the Trinity to the Passion, and may present the Cross as the revelation of the Trinity or as the Son's sacrifice within the Godhead (a 'Throne of Mercy' type of idea). The faint circular scheme in the lower part and the architectural and column-like drawing behind the triangle are probably show-through from the other side of the leaf or from other drawings on the page. They are not part of this diagram and are left uninterpreted.
evidence: Visible: an inverted triangle with a circle at each of its three corners, a central circle joined to the three corner circles by spokes, and a crucified figure with outstretched arms placed on the vertical axis between the central and bottom circles. This structure matches the Trinitarian triangle and shield diagrams of medieval theology. External: the identification of the nodes as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and of the centre as divine unity, comes from knowledge of the scutum fidei tradition; no legible labels confirm it. The link between the Crucifixion and the Trinity is a known iconographic combination. The background circular scheme and the architectural forms are uninterpreted because they look like bleed-through or an earlier drawing.
